name: MLIR
production_evidence: Triton uses MLIR as its backend (since v2.0)
XLA uses MLIR for some passes
TorchInductor uses MLIR for some transformations
strengths: Reusable compiler infrastructure: dialects, passes, and transformations are composable
Multi-level: can represent both high-level graph operations and low-level loop optimizations
Extensible: new dialects can be defined for domain-specific optimizations
Solves real problems: addresses software fragmentation in compiler development
Active development: weekly public meetings, large community, LLVM project governance
weaknesses: Not a source language: MLIR is explicitly not designed for end-users to write kernels in
Steep learning curve: understanding dialects, passes, and the pass manager requires significant compiler expertise
Complexity: the flexibility of MLIR makes it easy to create hard-to-debug compilation pipelines
Not a standalone tool: MLIR is infrastructure that must be integrated into a larger compiler
notes: MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation) is compiler infrastructure, not a standalone compiler. It provides a framework for building domain-specific compilers by defining dialects (sets of operations) and passes (transformations). MLIR's key innovation is the ability to represent computations at multiple levels of abstraction in a single IR, enabling gradual lowering from high-level graph operations to low-level machine code. MLIR explicitly does not handle register allocation or instruction scheduling (those are left to LLVM). The project is governed as part of the LLVM project and has weekly public meetings. For inference, MLIR is the backbone of Triton (since v2.0), IREE, and parts of XLA and TorchInductor. Its value is in enabling code reuse across these projects: a pass written for one dialect can be used by any compiler that includes that dialect.
